title: Leadership in digital compliance: how to manage technology responsibly and with confidence
summary: Discover how leadership in digital compliance brings together regulation, technology and business to manage risks and innovate responsibly.
body_markdown:
Leadership in digital compliance integrates regulation, technology, business and risk management so that organisations can innovate, make informed decisions and use technology responsibly and reliably.


## What is leadership in digital compliance and why is it important?


For a long time, digital compliance has been understood as a collection of specialised obligations. Data protection on the one hand, cybersecurity on the other, artificial intelligence in a still-emerging field, and sector-specific or contractual regulation across different teams and processes. This division makes sense from a technical and legal perspective, but is beginning to prove insufficient from the point of view of organisational governance.


Technology no longer plays a secondary role. It forms part of products and services, customer relationships, internal decision-making, people management, the supply chain and business continuity. When technology takes on such a structural presence, compliance cannot be limited to coming at the end of the process to check whether a decision is legally acceptable. It must be involved in the way the organisation decides, designs, prioritises and oversees.


This is where leadership takes on particular importance.


Talking about leadership in digital compliance does not simply mean discussing who leads a team or who has been assigned a formal responsibility. It means discussing the ability to guide an organisation in an environment of continuous technological and regulatory change. It means helping to ensure that digital decisions are sustainable, explainable and consistent with the company’s values, risks and responsibilities.


From a corporate perspective, this leadership helps ensure that access to digital technologies takes place securely, responsibly and with confidence. This approach aligns naturally with Telefónica’s ambition to facilitate citizens’ access to technology and to offer services whose quality is also measured by the trust of its customers.


## Why does the challenge of digital compliance go beyond simply knowing the regulations?


Digital regulation has proliferated and become increasingly specialised. The General Data Protection Regulation, the Artificial Intelligence Regulation, the NIS2 Directive, the Cyber Resilience Regulation, the Digital Services Act and the new European data rules address different risks and set out specific obligations. However, they share the same underlying principle: technology must be developed and used within a framework of accountability.


For an organisation, the challenge is not merely to identify which regulation applies. It lies in understanding how these obligations relate to one another and how they are put into practice.


An artificial intelligence system may raise issues relating to privacy, cybersecurity, intellectual property, transparency, consumer protection, labour rights and contractual liability. A connected product may require cybersecurity measures built into its design, proper vulnerability management, clear information for its users and effective governance of its supply chain. A security incident may trigger notification obligations, affect personal data, compromise the availability of essential services and have significant reputational consequences.


None of these issues can be fully managed from a single perspective.


For this reason, a mature digital compliance function should not aim to replace specialists. Privacy will continue to require professionals with in-depth knowledge of data protection. Cybersecurity will need technical teams capable of preventing, detecting and responding to incidents. Artificial intelligence will demand experts in data, models, product and architecture. But someone must be able to connect these pieces, identify the points of contact and provide a comprehensive view of the risk.


This is one of the key areas of leadership in digital compliance.


## How does leadership in digital compliance bridge the technical, legal and business functions?


One of the most common challenges in digital compliance is that the people involved do not always speak the same language. Technical teams may focus on the feasibility, performance or security of a solution.


The business side may prioritise opportunity, speed and customer experience. The legal department may focus on regulatory requirements and the allocation of responsibilities. Governing bodies need to understand the relevant risks without necessarily delving into every technical detail.


Leadership in digital compliance consists, to a large extent, of building bridges between these different languages.


It is not a question of oversimplifying complexity or turning every technological issue into a legal one. It is about asking the right questions and ensuring that decision-makers have sufficient information to make responsible decisions.


For example, a discussion about artificial intelligence should not begin solely by asking which tool to procure or what capabilities a particular model offers. It should also include questions such as what the intended purpose is, what data will be used, what decisions may be influenced by the system, what level of human oversight will be in place, what risks may affect people, and how the measures taken will be documented.


Similarly, a discussion about cybersecurity cannot focus solely on the existence of a vulnerability or the application of a patch. It must include the potential impact on services, customers, data, business continuity and the organisation’s obligations. The question is not merely whether a risk is technically possible, but also whether it is being properly understood, prioritised and managed.


A good digital compliance leader helps ensure these discussions take place before a problem arises.


## Why must compliance be embedded from the design stage?


For years, compliance has sometimes been viewed as a final-stage review function. The project is designed, the product is developed, the supplier is selected and, when everything is practically decided, legal or compliance validation is sought. This approach may be convenient in the short term, but it often leads to friction and costs when risks are identified too late.


In the digital sphere, being late has a particularly significant impact. Correcting an architecture, redesigning a data flow, incorporating security controls or modifying an artificial intelligence system once it has been deployed can be complex, costly and, in some cases, insufficient.


For this reason, leadership in digital compliance must promote a culture of early involvement. Compliance should not be an obstacle that appears at the end of the road, but a function that helps to navigate it more effectively from the outset.


This requires being closely involved in innovation, product, procurement, technology and business processes. It requires understanding how projects are actually developed, what decisions are made at each stage and where proportionate controls can be incorporated. It also requires avoiding purely abstract responses. A policy or a contractual clause is necessary, but it is no substitute for an assessment process, a clear allocation of responsibilities or effective oversight.


The aim should not be to add layers of bureaucracy. It should be to integrate compliance into decision-making so that the organisation can innovate with greater confidence.


This early integration is particularly important for companies that aim to offer innovative and competitive technology services. Sustainable innovation requires that security, accountability and trust form part of the design process, rather than being incorporated only once the product or service has already been defined.


## How does digital compliance help to identify and highlight risks?


An essential part of leadership is to bring to light what might otherwise remain scattered or go unnoticed. Digital risks are often cross-cutting, cumulative and difficult to perceive until they materialise.


A seemingly limited tool may be extended to new uses. A supplier may make changes to its terms and conditions or technology. A dataset collected for a specific purpose may end up being used in a different context. A product may rely on third-party components, libraries or services that introduce new vulnerabilities. An automated decision may have significant effects on people even when human intervention is still formally present.


Leadership in digital compliance involves identifying these connections and communicating them to the bodies and teams that need to take action. To do this, it is not enough simply to describe a regulatory obligation. It is necessary to explain the risk in understandable terms: what might happen, who might be affected, what the consequences would be, and what decision is required.


In this regard, traceability is essential. Organisations must be able to explain which system they use, for what purpose, what risks they identified, what measures they adopted, who assumed each responsibility and how the model’s performance is reviewed. Documentation should not be viewed merely as a formal requirement. It is a tool for governance, learning and demonstrating that decisions have been made in an informed manner.


## How are risks prioritised in digital compliance?


In such a broad regulatory environment, no organisation can manage all issues with the same level of intensity. Not all AI systems present the same level of risk. Not all suppliers are equally significant. Not all vulnerabilities require the same response. Not all products or services have the same impact on customers, users or critical infrastructure.


Leadership in digital compliance requires sound judgement in prioritisation.


A risk-based approach allows efforts to be concentrated where they are truly needed. This involves establishing mechanisms to classify use cases, products, services and suppliers; defining when each function should intervene; escalating decisions that may have significant consequences; and reviewing controls when technology, context or the level of exposure changes.


Prioritising does not mean ignoring minor risks. It means managing them proportionately and devoting greater attention to those scenarios that may have a more significant impact on people’s rights, security, service continuity or trust in the organisation.


The maturity of a compliance model is not measured by the number of controls it contains, but by its ability to distinguish between what is essential and what is incidental, and to act consistently.


## What role do governing bodies play in managing digital risks?


Technological complexity does not absolve those who lead an organisation of their responsibility. On the contrary, it makes informed oversight all the more necessary. Boards of directors and senior management do not need to become technical specialists, but they must understand the main digital risks, approve the relevant courses of action and receive sufficient information on how the controls operate.


This is particularly evident in areas such as cybersecurity, artificial intelligence and digital resilience. Decisions regarding investment, innovation, suppliers, business continuity, reputational risks and risk tolerance are not purely technical decisions. They are governance decisions.


Leadership in digital compliance plays a particularly valuable role here: transforming regulatory and technical complexity into useful information for decision-making. This involves providing a clear overview of the risks, the applicable obligations, the measures already in place, and the issues requiring a decision or enhanced oversight.


It also involves avoiding a false sense of security. Having policies, committees or procedures in place does not, in itself, guarantee an effective framework. What matters is that these tools work in practice, that responsibilities are clear, that incidents are escalated appropriately, and that the organisation can learn from its mistakes


## How does digital compliance help to build trust?


Ultimately, leadership in digital compliance is not about preventing the use of technology. It is about helping to use it in a way that builds trust.


The trust of customers, who expect their data, communications and services to be protected. The trust of employees, who need to understand how the digital tools used in their working environment might affect them. The trust of regulators and authorities, who expect organisations to be able to demonstrate that they manage their risks effectively. And, finally, the trust of the organisation itself, which needs to innovate without losing sight of its responsibilities.


Digital compliance must not be limited to answering the question: ‘Can we do this?’. Its most valuable contribution lies in helping to answer other questions: ‘Should we do it this way?’, ‘What risks should we accept?’, ‘What safeguards do we need?’ and ‘How do we demonstrate that we are acting responsibly?’.


Leading in digital compliance means recognising that technology is not just a matter of efficiency or innovation. It is also a matter of governance, responsibility and trust. And, precisely for that reason, it will be one of the most important capabilities for organisations in the coming years.


For Telefónica, customer trust is also a key benchmark for measuring service quality. Within this framework, digital compliance contributes to innovation that not only broadens access to digital technologies but also incorporates the necessary safeguards to ensure they are used responsibly.


## FREQUENTLY ASKED QUESTIONS


**What is digital compliance?**


Digital compliance is the approach that integrates the obligations and risks related to data protection, cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, sector-specific regulation and other areas linked to the use of technology. Its purpose is to embed accountability into the way an organisation makes decisions, designs processes, sets priorities and carries out oversight.


**What is the purpose of leadership in digital compliance?**


It serves to bridge the technical, legal and business perspectives, identify the relationships between different risks and provide a comprehensive view that facilitates responsible and informed decision-making


**Why must compliance be built in from the design stage?**


Because identifying risks once a product, system or project has already been developed may necessitate changes to architectures, data flows, security controls or artificial intelligence systems. Incorporating it from the earliest stages allows for the application of proportionate controls and reduces friction later on.


**What risks should an artificial intelligence project consider?**


It may raise issues relating to privacy, cybersecurity, intellectual property, transparency, consumer protection, labour rights and contractual liability. The purpose, the data used, the decisions affected, human oversight and the potential effects on individuals must also be analysed.


**What are the responsibilities of the governing bodies?**


They must understand the main digital risks, approve the relevant courses of action and receive sufficient information about the controls. Decisions relating to investment, innovation, suppliers, business continuity and risk tolerance form part of the organisation’s governance.


**How does digital compliance build trust?**


It helps to protect data, communications and services; to explain the impact of digital tools; to demonstrate effective risk management; and to innovate whilst remaining mindful of the organisation’s responsibilities.
